original_question: Do there exist invariant perfect sets, meaning nonempty compact invariant sets that are transversally totally discontinuous, for differential equations of class C^2 on orientable two-dimensional manifolds?
target_in_paper: Section 6.4, "The existence of nontrivial minimal sets". This paper does not contain a Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3; the draft is targeting the fourth problem in Peixoto’s list of open problems.
correct_elements: The draft is already very close to the paper’s actual question. It correctly identifies the object of interest (invariant perfect sets), preserves the paper’s description of such sets as nonempty, compact, invariant, and transversally totally discontinuous, keeps the regularity class C^2, and keeps the scope restricted to orientable two-dimensional manifolds.
missing_details: The paper places the question under the heading "The existence of nontrivial minimal sets"; that heading gives the intended Denjoy/Poincare context, even though the sentence itself is phrased in terms of invariant perfect sets.
A fully stand-alone version may clarify that a "differential equation of class C^2 on an orientable two-dimensional manifold" is the flow generated by a C^2 vector field on such a manifold.

If complete self-containment is desired, "transversally totally discontinuous" should be glossed via intersections with local transversals; Section 6.4 itself does not spell this out, so the draft leaves that technical phrase implicit.
A faithful rewrite should not add extra ambient hypotheses not stated in Section 6.4, such as compactness, closedness, connectedness, or boundarylessness of the manifold.
The nearby context records that Schwartz later solved the problem negatively; that is important historical context but is not part of the problem statement itself.
refined_question: Do invariant perfect sets—that is, nonempty, compact, invariant sets that are transversally totally discontinuous—exist for differential equations of class C^2 on orientable two-dimensional manifolds?
justification: The draft is aiming at the exact sentence in Section 6.4 rather than any labeled conjecture or theorem, since arXiv:1808.10571 is a historical essay organized by sections and numbered problems, not by Conjecture 1.1 / Proposition 1.2 / Theorem 1.3. The nearest official formulation is the Section 6.4 question itself, which your draft follows almost verbatim. Section 4.1 gives the immediate mathematical context by recalling Denjoy’s example of a closed invariant set that is transversally a Cantor set and is called "minimal non-trivial," which explains the section title. Section 7 records that this exact problem was later solved in the negative direction by A. J. Schwartz. Because Section 6.4 does not itself impose extra assumptions on the ambient manifold, the refined version keeps the scope exactly at the level of the paper and does not broaden it.
